claim: The σ subunit of bacterial RNA polymerase (RNAP) confers on the enzyme the ability to initiate promoter-specific transcription.
source: The σ subunit of bacterial RNA polymerase (RNAP) confers on the enzyme the ability to initiate promoter-specific transcription.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field of bacterial transcription, representing established scientific consensus.

claim: σ factors are generally classified as initiation factors.
source: Although σ factors are generally classified as initiation factors, σ can also remain associated with, and modulate the behavior of, RNAP during elongation.
evidence: This represents the historical classification of σ factors in the field.

claim: σ can remain associated with and modulate the behavior of RNAP during elongation.
source: Although σ factors are generally classified as initiation factors, σ can also remain associated with, and modulate the behavior of, RNAP during elongation.
evidence: This is supported by prior research in the field as indicated by the context of the manuscript.

claim: The primary σ factor in Escherichia coli, σ70, can function as an elongation factor in vivo by loading directly onto the transcription elongation complex (TEC) in trans.
source: Here we establish that the primary σ factor in Escherichia coli, σ70, can function as an elongation factor in vivo by loading directly onto the transcription elongation complex (TEC) in trans.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: σ70 can bind in trans to TECs that emanate from a σ70-dependent promoter.
source: We demonstrate that σ70 can bind in trans to TECs that emanate from either a σ70-dependent promoter or a promoter that is controlled by an alternative σ factor.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: σ70 can bind in trans to TECs that emanate from a promoter that is controlled by an alternative σ factor.
source: We demonstrate that σ70 can bind in trans to TECs that emanate from either a σ70-dependent promoter or a promoter that is controlled by an alternative σ factor.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figures 2, 3, and 4.

claim: Binding of σ70 to the TEC in trans can have a particularly large impact on the dynamics of transcription elongation during stationary phase.
source: We further demonstrate that binding of σ70 to the TEC in trans can have a particularly large impact on the dynamics of transcription elongation during stationary phase.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The primary σ factor can exert direct effects on the composition of the entire transcriptome, not just that portion that is produced under the control of σ70-dependent promoters.
source: Our findings establish a mechanism whereby the primary σ factor can exert direct effects on the composition of the entire transcriptome, not just that portion that is produced under the control of σ70-dependent promoters.
evidence: This is inferred from the finding that σ70 can bind to TECs initiated by alternative σ factors.

claim: All bacteria contain a primary σ factor that directs transcription from the major class of bacterial promoters.
source: All bacteria contain a primary σ factor that directs transcription from the major class of bacterial promoters; in addition, most bacteria contain multiple alternative σ factors that direct transcription from specialized promoters in response to stress or alterations in growth state (Gruber and Gross, 2003; Osterberg et al., 2011; Guo and Gross, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Most bacteria contain multiple alternative σ factors that direct transcription from specialized promoters in response to stress or alterations in growth state.
source: All bacteria contain a primary σ factor that directs transcription from the major class of bacterial promoters; in addition, most bacteria contain multiple alternative σ factors that direct transcription from specialized promoters in response to stress or alterations in growth state (Gruber and Gross, 2003; Osterberg et al., 2011; Guo and Gross, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Escherichia coli σ70 recognizes promoters that are defined by two conserved hexameric DNA sequence elements termed the −10 and the −35 elements.
source: Among the best-studied primary σ factors is Escherichia coli σ70, which recognizes promoters that are defined by two conserved hexameric DNA sequence elements termed the −10 and the −35 elements (consensus sequences: TATAAT and TTGACA, respectively).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of bacterial transcription.

claim: The consensus sequence of the −10 element is TATAAT.
source: Among the best-studied primary σ factors is Escherichia coli σ70, which recognizes promoters that are defined by two conserved hexameric DNA sequence elements termed the −10 and the −35 elements (consensus sequences: TATAAT and TTGACA, respectively).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: The consensus sequence of the −35 element is TTGACA.
source: Among the best-studied primary σ factors is Escherichia coli σ70, which recognizes promoters that are defined by two conserved hexameric DNA sequence elements termed the −10 and the −35 elements (consensus sequences: TATAAT and TTGACA, respectively).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Members of the σ70 family share a conserved 4-domain architecture.
source: Members of the σ70 family share a conserved 4-domain architecture, with domain 2 contacting the −10 element and domain 4 contacting the −35 element (Gross et al., 1998; Paget and Helmann, 2003; Feklistov et al., 2014; Paget, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Domain 2 of σ70 contacts the −10 element.
source: Members of the σ70 family share a conserved 4-domain architecture, with domain 2 contacting the −10 element and domain 4 contacting the −35 element (Gross et al., 1998; Paget and Helmann, 2003; Feklistov et al., 2014; Paget, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Domain 4 of σ70 contacts the −35 element.
source: Members of the σ70 family share a conserved 4-domain architecture, with domain 2 contacting the −10 element and domain 4 contacting the −35 element (Gross et al., 1998; Paget and Helmann, 2003; Feklistov et al., 2014; Paget, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: E. coli has six alternative σ factors.
source: E. coli also has six alternative σ factors, five of which are members of the σ70 family and recognize similarly positioned promoter elements using the counterparts of σ70 domains 2 and 4.
evidence: This is established knowledge about E. coli.

claim: Five of E. coli's alternative σ factors are members of the σ70 family.
source: E. coli also has six alternative σ factors, five of which are members of the σ70 family and recognize similarly positioned promoter elements using the counterparts of σ70 domains 2 and 4.
evidence: This is established knowledge about E. coli.

claim: Most alternative σ factors exhibit highly restricted promoter specificity.
source: Most alternative σ factors exhibit highly restricted promoter specificity (Koo et al., 2009b; Rhodius et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Genes that are responsive to disparate physiological inputs often carry two or more promoters that are recognized by distinct σ factors.
source: Thus, genes that are responsive to disparate physiological inputs often carry two or more promoters that are recognized by distinct σ factors (Wade et al., 2006; Gama-Castro et al., 2008; Cho et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The release of σ from the transcription complex is not required for entry into the elongation phase of transcription.
source: In particular, multiple studies have shown that the release of σ from the transcription complex is not required for entry into the elongation phase of transcription (reviewed in Mooney et al., 2005; Perdue and Roberts, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: The functional properties of a transcription elongation complex (TEC) containing σ differ from the properties of a TEC that does not contain σ.
source: Furthermore, the functional properties of a transcription elongation complex (TEC) containing σ differ from the properties of a TEC that does not contain σ.
evidence: This is supported by the subsequent examples and citations provided in the text.

claim: TEC-associated σ70 can induce transcription pausing by engaging promoter −10-like sequence elements within transcribed regions.
source: For example, TEC-associated σ70 can induce transcription pausing by engaging promoter −10-like sequence elements within transcribed regions (Ring et al., 1996; Brodolin et al., 2004; Nickels et al., 2004; Hatoum and Roberts, 2008; Deighan et al., 2011; Perdue and Roberts, 2011), a phenomenon that was first uncovered in the context of the bacteriophage λ late gene promoter (reviewed in Roberts et al., 1998; Perdue and Roberts, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: σ70-dependent pausing occurs due to an interaction between the −10-like element and domain 2 of TEC-associated σ70.
source: This pausing occurs due to an interaction between the −10-like element and domain 2 of TEC-associated σ70 (the same domain of σ70 that binds the promoter −10 element during transcription initiation).
evidence: This is based on prior research establishing the mechanism of σ70-dependent pausing.

claim: The presence or absence of σ can alter the accessibility of the TEC to elongation factors, including the λ Q protein and RfaH.
source: In addition, the presence or absence of σ can alter the accessibility of the TEC to elongation factors, including the λ Q protein and RfaH (Roberts et al., 1998; Nickels et al., 2002, 2006; Sevostyanova et al., 2008), and can influence the ability of RNAP to reinitiate transcription at certain promoters (Bar-Nahum and Nudler, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The presence or absence of σ can influence the ability of RNAP to reinitiate transcription at certain promoters.
source: In addition, the presence or absence of σ can alter the accessibility of the TEC to elongation factors, including the λ Q protein and RfaH (Roberts et al., 1998; Nickels et al., 2002, 2006; Sevostyanova et al., 2008), and can influence the ability of RNAP to reinitiate transcription at certain promoters (Bar-Nahum and Nudler, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Initial-transcribed-region −10-like elements induce early elongation pausing because they are recognized by TECs that have not yet released the σ70 that was used during initiation.
source: Initial-transcribed-region −10-like elements, such as those associated with the λ late promoters and the late promoters of other lambdoid phages, induce early elongation pausing because they are recognized by TECs that have not yet released the σ70 that was used during initiation (Marr et al., 2001; Mukhopadhyay et al., 2001; Nickels et al., 2004; Kapanidis et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Promoter-proximal σ70-dependent pause elements function to inhibit σ70 loss during the earliest stages of elongation, increasing the σ70 content of downstream TECs.
source: In prior work, we showed that such promoter-proximal σ70-dependent pause elements also function to inhibit σ70 loss during the earliest stages of elongation, increasing the σ70 content of downstream TECs (Deighan et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: The presence of a promoter-proximal pause element facilitates the retention of σ70 in the TEC and substantially enhances the extent of pausing induced by a downstream pause element both in vitro and in vivo.
source: This effect can be detected using a template that carries a second pause element positioned downstream of a promoter-proximal pause element; specifically, the presence of the promoter-proximal pause element facilitates the retention of σ70 in the TEC and thus substantially enhances the extent of pausing induced by the downstream pause element both in vitro and in vivo (Deighan et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: In vitro studies have established that transcribed region −10-like elements can be recognized by a σ70 subunit that was not present during initiation, but rather joined the TEC by loading in trans during elongation.
source: Although promoter −10-like elements that induce transcription pausing can be recognized by a σ70 subunit that has been retained in the TEC after promoter escape, in vitro studies have established that transcribed region −10-like elements can also be recognized by a σ70 subunit that was not present during initiation, but rather joined the TEC by loading in trans during elongation.
evidence: This is supported by the subsequent citations to in vitro studies.

claim: The efficiency of pausing induced by transcribed region −10-like elements can be increased in vitro by increasing the concentration of free σ70 in the transcription reactions.
source: Thus, it has been shown that the efficiency of pausing induced by transcribed region −10-like elements can be increased in vitro by increasing the concentration of free σ70 in the transcription reactions (Mooney and Landick, 2003; Sevostyanova et al., 2008; Deighan et al., 2011; Sevostyanova et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior in vitro studies.

claim: The relative abundance of a ∼35-nt pause RNA increased approximately fivefold when σ70 was overproduced by a factor of approximately 7.
source: We found that the relative abundance of a ∼35-nt pause RNA (see Deighan et al., 2011) increased ∼fivefold when σ70 was overproduced by a factor of ∼7, compared to that observed in cells containing chromosomally encoded σ70 only (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The ∼35-nt pause RNA was barely detected with or without excess σ70 using a control template carrying base-pair substitutions that disrupt sequence-specific recognition of the transcribed-region −10-like element by σ70 region 2.
source: Furthermore, the ∼35-nt pause RNA was barely detected with or without excess σ70 using a control template carrying base-pair substitutions that disrupt sequence-specific recognition of the transcribed-region −10-like element by σ70 region 2 (Deighan et al., 2011) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Pausing of the TEC under the control of a −10-like element within a transcribed region is sensitive to the intracellular concentration of σ70.
source: We conclude that pausing of the TEC under the control of a −10-like element within a transcribed region is sensitive to the intracellular concentration of σ70, suggesting that σ70 can access the TEC in trans, in vivo.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing increased pausing with σ70 overproduction.

claim: The presence of the promoter-proximal −10-like element resulted in a substantial increase (approximately ninefold) in the relative abundance of the ∼35-nt pause species.
source: Consistent with previous findings (Deighan et al., 2011), the presence of the promoter-proximal −10-like element resulted in a substantial increase (∼ninefold) in the relative abundance of the ∼35-nt pause species (compare Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1A and 1B.

claim: When σ70 was overproduced, the relative abundance of the ∼35-nt pause species increased further (approximately 1.5 fold) on the template with a promoter-proximal pause element.
source: Nonetheless, when σ70 was overproduced, the relative abundance of the ∼35-nt pause species increased further (∼1.5 fold; Figure 1B, middle and bottom panels), indicating that the effect of the promoter-proximal −10-like element on the σ70 content of downstream TECs is not saturating.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The effect of the promoter-proximal −10-like element on the σ70 content of downstream TECs is not saturating.
source: Nonetheless, when σ70 was overproduced, the relative abundance of the ∼35-nt pause species increased further (∼1.5 fold; Figure 1B, middle and bottom panels), indicating that the effect of the promoter-proximal −10-like element on the σ70 content of downstream TECs is not saturating.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that σ70 overproduction further increases pausing even in the presence of a promoter-proximal pause element.

claim: σ28 is an alternative σ factor that controls the expression of genes involved in flagellar synthesis.
source: To address this possibility we generated a new template that carried a promoter recognized by RNAP holoenzyme carrying σ28, an alternative σ factor that controls the expression of genes involved in flagellar synthesis (Chilcott and Hughes, 2000; Koo et al., 2009a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Addition of σ70 to in vitro transcription reactions using a σ28-dependent promoter resulted in the appearance of a cluster of RNAs approximately 35-nt in length.
source: Addition of σ70 to the transcription reactions resulted in the appearance of a cluster of RNAs ∼35-nt in length (Figure 2, compare lanes 4–6 with lanes 1–3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The approximately 35-nt RNAs were not observed when reactions were performed using a control template carrying disruptive base-pair substitutions within the transcribed-region −10-like element.
source: These RNAs were not observed when reactions were performed using a control template carrying disruptive base-pair substitutions within the transcribed-region −10-like element (Figure 2B, lanes 7–12).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Appearance of the cluster of approximately 35-nt RNAs is strictly dependent on transcription that initiates from Ptar under the control of σ28.
source: A set of reactions performed in the presence of σ70 but in the absence of σ28 confirmed that appearance of the cluster of ∼35-nt RNAs is strictly dependent on transcription that initiates from Ptar under the control of σ28 (Figure 2B, lanes 13–15).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Free σ70 can bind to TECs on a σ28-controlled transcription unit in vitro.
source: We conclude that the ∼35-nt RNAs are pause RNAs that arise due to the ability of σ70 to bind TECs generated via transcription initiating at Ptar under the control of σ28. These findings therefore indicate that free σ70 can bind to TECs on a σ28-controlled transcription unit in vitro.
evidence: This is inferred from the in vitro experimental data showing σ70-dependent pausing on σ28-initiated transcripts.

claim: Transcripts emanating from Ptar were detected only in cells carrying the plasmid that directed the synthesis of excess σ28.
source: We found that transcripts emanating from Ptar were detected only in cells carrying the plasmid that directed the synthesis of excess σ28 (Figure 3A, compare lanes 2–5 with lane 6).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: In the presence of excess σ28 but in the absence of excess σ70, a small amount of an RNA species that migrated between the 30-nt and 40-nt RNA markers was detected.
source: Furthermore, in the presence of excess σ28 but in the absence of excess σ70, we detected a small amount of an RNA species that migrated between the 30-nt and 40-nt RNA markers (Figure 3A, lane 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The relative abundance of the approximately 35-nt RNA from the Ptar template was increased approximately sevenfold when σ70 was overproduced by a factor of approximately 3.
source: We found that the relative abundance of this ∼35-nt RNA was increased ∼sevenfold when σ70 was overproduced by a factor of ∼3 (Figure 3A, compare lanes 2 and 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The approximately 35-nt RNA was not detected in cells containing the mutant Ptar template carrying base-pair substitutions in the transcribed-region −10-like element.
source: In addition, the ∼35-nt RNA was not detected in cells containing the mutant Ptar template carrying base-pair substitutions in the transcribed-region −10-like element (Figure 3A, lanes 4 and 5).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: A major fraction of the approximately 35-nt RNA species, but not the full-length terminated transcript, was immunoprecipitated with an antibody against FLAG.
source: The results indicate that a major fraction of the ∼35-nt RNA species, but not the full-length terminated transcript, was immunoprecipitated with an antibody against FLAG whether the cells lacked or contained plasmid encoded overproduced σ70 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: A major fraction of the approximately 35-nt RNA species is RNAP-associated.
source: Thus, we conclude that a major fraction of the ∼35-nt RNA species, but not the full-length terminated transcript, is RNAP-associated.
evidence: This is inferred from the immunoprecipitation data showing co-precipitation with FLAG-tagged RNAP.

claim: σ70 can access the TEC in trans, in vivo.
source: We therefore conclude that the ∼35-nt RNA produced from the Ptar template in vivo represents a pause RNA that arises due to the ability of σ70 to bind TECs generated under the control of σ28. Furthermore, our ability to detect σ70-dependent pause species produced under the control of a promoter that is recognized by an alternative σ factor enables us unambiguously to identify pausing that is mediated by trans-loaded σ70. Thus, our findings establish that σ70 can access the TEC in trans, in vivo.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by the experimental data from Figures 1-4.

claim: During the exponential phase of growth the extent of pausing due to chromosomally encoded trans-loaded σ70 appeared to be low (relative abundance of the approximately 35-nt RNA was <5%).
source: Although experiments using the Ptar template revealed that σ70 trans loading is detectable even in the absence of σ70 overproduction, we found that during the exponential phase of growth the extent of pausing due to chromosomally encoded trans-loaded σ70 appeared to be low (Figures 3A and 4A; the relative abundance of the ∼35-nt RNA was <5%).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3A and 4A.

claim: When RNA was harvested from stationary phase cells containing the Ptar template, the relative abundance of the approximately 35-nt RNA was approximately 50%.
source: However, when we harvested RNA from stationary phase cells containing the Ptar template, we found that the relative abundance of the ∼35-nt RNA was ∼50% (Figure 4A, lane 3), which was reduced to ∼10% when the transcribed-region −10-like element was mutated (Figure 4A, lane 5).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The relative abundance of the approximately 35-nt RNA from the mutant Ptar template in stationary phase was reduced to approximately 10%.
source: However, when we harvested RNA from stationary phase cells containing the Ptar template, we found that the relative abundance of the ∼35-nt RNA was ∼50% (Figure 4A, lane 3), which was reduced to ∼10% when the transcribed-region −10-like element was mutated (Figure 4A, lane 5).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The approximately 35-nt RNAs detected from the Ptar template during stationary phase were RNAP-associated.
source: Furthermore, like those detected during exponential phase, the ∼35-nt RNAs detected from the Ptar template during stationary phase were RNAP-associated (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The relative abundance of pause RNAs that arise due to σ70 trans loading varies with growth-phase.
source: We conclude that the relative abundance of pause RNAs that arise due to σ70 trans loading varies with growth-phase.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of exponential and stationary phase data.

claim: The cell extracts prepared from exponential and stationary phase cultures contained comparable amounts of σ70.
source: The results indicated that the cell extracts prepared from exponential and stationary phase cultures contained comparable amounts of σ70 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The growth phase-dependent increase in the abundance of the approximately 35-nt pause RNAs is not a consequence of an increase in the total cellular concentration of σ70.
source: We conclude that the growth phase-dependent increase in the abundance of the ∼35-nt pause RNAs is not a consequence of an increase in the total cellular concentration of σ70.
evidence: This is inferred from the Western blot data showing comparable σ70 levels in exponential and stationary phase.

claim: The half-life of the approximately 35-nt pause RNA was greater in stationary phase than in exponential phase.
source: We found that the half-life of the ∼35-nt pause RNA was greater in stationary phase than in exponential phase (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B using rifampicin treatment.

claim: The full-length terminated transcript was at least as stable in stationary phase as in exponential phase.
source: In addition, the full-length terminated transcript was at least as stable in stationary phase as in exponential phase (Figure 4B), excluding the possibility that the increase in the relative abundance of the pause RNA might simply reflect a destabilization of the full-length transcript in stationary phase.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The extent of pausing on the Ptar template due to trans-loaded σ70 varies with growth phase, at least in part, due to an increase in the half-life of the pause.
source: Thus, our findings indicate that the extent of pausing on the Ptar template due to trans-loaded σ70 varies with growth phase, at least in part, due to an increase in the half-life of the pause.
evidence: This is inferred from the rifampicin chase experiments showing differential pause RNA stability.

claim: At least two distinct σ factors can influence the functional properties of a transcription complex during the transcription cycle in vivo: one during initiation and one (or more) during elongation.
source: Our findings indicate that at least two distinct σ factors can influence the functional properties of a transcription complex during the transcription cycle in vivo: one during initiation and one (or more) during elongation.
evidence: This is inferred from the finding that σ28 directs initiation while σ70 can bind in trans during elongation.

claim: There are two pathways whereby σ70 can access the TEC in vivo: a pathway that operates in cis and a pathway that operates in trans.
source: The results presented here, coupled with prior work (Shimamoto et al., 1986; Ring et al., 1996; Bar-Nahum and Nudler, 2001; Mukhopadhyay et al., 2001; Brodolin et al., 2004; Nickels et al., 2004; Wade and Struhl, 2004; Kapanidis et al., 2005; Raffaelle et al., 2005; Reppas et al., 2006; Mooney et al., 2009; Deighan et al., 2011) define two pathways whereby σ70 can access the TEC in vivo, a pathway that operates in cis and a pathway that operates in trans (Figure 5).
evidence: This is inferred from the current study's data combined with prior literature.

claim: The cis-acting pathway depends on retention in the TEC of the σ70 that was used during initiation.
source: The cis-acting pathway depends on retention in the TEC of the σ70 that was used during initiation, with the extent of σ70 retention being modulated by the sequence of the initial transcribed region (Figure 5A) (Deighan et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by prior work cited and illustrated in Figure 5A.

claim: The cis-acting (retention) pathway is necessarily restricted to transcription units controlled by σ70-dependent promoters.
source: Thus, the cis-acting (retention) pathway is necessarily restricted to transcription units controlled by σ70-dependent promoters.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the definition of the cis-acting pathway.

claim: The trans-acting pathway is potentially operative on all transcription units.
source: In contrast, the trans-acting pathway identified in this study, which can be functionally defined by its sensitivity to the intracellular concentration of σ70, is potentially operative on all transcription units (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is inferred from the demonstration that σ70 can bind in trans to TECs initiated by alternative σ factors.

claim: The cis-acting and trans-acting pathways can function in concert.
source: Moreover, the two pathways can function in concert.
evidence: This is supported by the data showing that σ70 trans loading can augment pausing even when a promoter-proximal pause element is present.

claim: σ70 trans loading can increase the σ70 content of TECs generated under the control of a σ70-dependent promoter even in the presence of an initial-transcribed-region σ70-dependent pause element that augments σ70 retention.
source: Thus, we found that σ70 trans loading can increase the σ70 content of TECs generated under the control of a σ70-dependent promoter even in the presence of an initial-transcribed-region σ70-dependent pause element that augments σ70 retention.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Pausing mediated by chromosomally encoded trans-loaded σ70 was detectable during the exponential phase of growth and this pausing became more prominent during stationary phase.
source: We found that the effects of trans-loaded σ70 on pausing varied with growth phase. In particular, pausing mediated by chromosomally encoded trans-loaded σ70 was detectable during the exponential phase of growth and this pausing became more prominent during stationary phase.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The increase in pause half-life in stationary phase might be due to a drop in the intracellular NTP concentrations as nutrients are depleted and the cells enter stationary phase.
source: We speculate that this increase in pause half-life might be due to a drop in the intracellular NTP concentrations as nutrients are depleted and the cells enter stationary phase (Buckstein et al., 2008).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning supported by a citation about NTP concentrations.

claim: RNAP holoenzyme purified from stationary phase cells produced a substantially higher fraction of σ70-containing TECs than did RNAP holoenzyme purified from exponentially growing cells.
source: In particular, the authors of this study found that RNAP holoenzyme purified from stationary phase cells produced a substantially higher fraction of σ70-containing TECs than did RNAP holoenzyme purified from exponentially growing cells, possibly suggesting that the stationary phase RNAP core enzyme binds σ70 more tightly.
evidence: This is a finding from a prior study being discussed in the context of the current results.

claim: A potential pause species was detectable above background in stationary phase cells even when the transcribed-region −10-like element was mutated.
source: We note that the effect of growth phase on the relative abundance of pause RNAs may not be limited to σ70–dependent pausing. In fact, our experiments revealed a potential pause species that was detectable above background in stationary phase cells even when the transcribed-region −10-like element was mutated (Figure 4A, lane 5).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The pause RNA detected with the mutated −10-like element arises due to the presence of an overlapping consensus pause element that is recognized by the core RNAP (G–10Y–1G+1).
source: We suggest that this RNA arises due to the presence of an overlapping consensus pause element that is recognized by the core RNAP (G–10Y–1G+1; see Figure 2A) (Herbert et al., 2006; Larson et al., 2014; Vvedenskaya et al., 2014) and is not disrupted by the mutations in the −10-like element.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning supported by citations about core RNAP pause elements.

claim: σ70 trans loading might enable the cell to integrate signals transmitted via σ70 and an alternative σ factor to modulate gene expression within a single transcription unit under the control of a non σ70–dependent promoter.
source: Such 'σ cross regulation' might enable the cell to integrate signals transmitted via σ70 and an alternative σ factor to modulate gene expression within a single transcription unit under the control of a non σ70–dependent promoter.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about the potential biological significance of the findings.

claim: σ70 trans loading can cause the TEC to pause, which is expected to influence transcription output directly in a manner that depends on pause half-life.
source: In principle there are several ways that σ70 trans loading might modulate gene expression. First, as shown here, σ70 trans loading can cause the TEC to pause, which is expected to influence transcription output directly in a manner that depends on pause half-life (and, as suggested by our results shown in Figure 4, may become particularly relevant in stationary phase).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data and general knowledge about transcription pausing.

claim: σ70–dependent pausing might influence gene expression indirectly, by facilitating engagement of regulatory factors, influencing formation of RNA secondary structures, or influencing translation.
source: σ70–dependent pausing might also influence gene expression indirectly, by facilitating engagement of regulatory factors, influencing formation of RNA secondary structures, or influencing translation (Roberts et al., 1998; Wickiser et al., 2005; Landick, 2006; Pan and Sosnick, 2006; Lemay et al., 2011; Perdrizet et al., 2012; Larson et al., 2014; Nechooshtan et al., 2014; Belogurov and Artsimovitch, 2015).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: σ70 trans loading might impede the accessibility of the TEC to other elongation factors such as NusG or RfaH, which share the same primary binding site on RNAP.
source: Second, σ70 trans loading might impede the accessibility of the TEC to other elongation factors such as NusG or RfaH, which share the same primary binding site on RNAP (Sevostyanova et al., 2008; Mooney et al., 2009).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: All experiments were performed in E. coli strain MG1655 or SG110.
source: All experiments were performed in E. coli strain MG1655 or SG110 (Vvedenskaya et al., 2014) in which the chromosomal rpoC gene is fused to a 3xFLAG epitope tag-encoding sequence.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the strains used.

claim: In strain SG110, the chromosomal rpoC gene is fused to a 3xFLAG epitope tag-encoding sequence.
source: All experiments were performed in E. coli strain MG1655 or SG110 (Vvedenskaya et al., 2014) in which the chromosomal rpoC gene is fused to a 3xFLAG epitope tag-encoding sequence.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the strain construction.
